title: Wisconsin Physicist Francis Halzen Wins Nobel for Turning a Cubic Kilometer of South Pole Ice Into a Neutrino Detector
byline: Avery Porter Published: Oct 07 2026, 6:40 PM EDT
excerpt: Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for IceCube, a South Pole ice detector that catches neutrinos from the universe’s most violent places.
content:
A scientist who spent decades convincing colleagues that the Antarctic ice sheet could serve as a telescope has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize on Tuesday, Oct. 6, to Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin-Madison for his work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from beyond Earth, Forbes reported.

Halzen, 82, receives the full prize of 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million, and will accept it in Stockholm on Dec. 10, according to Physics World.

The award honors a detector unlike any other on Earth. IceCube is not a dish or a mirror pointed at the sky. It is a cubic kilometer of ancient, crystal-clear ice at the bottom of the planet, wired with thousands of light sensors that wait for one of the rarest events in physics.

A Particle That Passes Through Almost Everything

Neutrinos are tiny subatomic particles with almost no mass and no electric charge. They are made in enormous numbers by the Sun, by nuclear reactions and by violent cosmic events, and trillions pass through every person's body each second without leaving a trace.

That ghostly nature is what makes them valuable to astronomers. Light from distant objects can be absorbed by dust or bent by magnetic fields. Neutrinos travel in straight lines across billions of light-years and arrive carrying information from places light cannot escape, such as the cores of exploding stars and the regions around black holes.

The same property makes them extremely hard to catch. Only a vanishingly small fraction of neutrinos ever bump into an atom. To record enough of those collisions, a detector has to be enormous.

The Nobel Committee for Physics described the result of Halzen's work in its announcement. "Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," the committee said.

Building a Telescope Inside the Antarctic Ice Sheet

The South Pole offered a solution. The ice there is more than a mile thick, very clear and almost completely dark at depth. When a neutrino does strike an atom in the ice, it produces a charged particle that gives off a faint flash of blue light. Sensors buried in the dark ice can record that flash and trace where the neutrino came from.

According to the IceCube collaboration's fact sheet, the observatory holds 5,160 digital optical modules strung along 86 cables. The sensors sit between 1,450 and 2,450 meters below the surface, roughly 0.9 to 1.5 miles down. Crews built it over seven years, from 2004 to 2010, working only during the brief Antarctic summer from November to February.

Each hole was melted with hot water, a process that took about 48 hours per hole and roughly 200,000 gallons of meltwater. The finished detector fills enough ice to fill about a million swimming pools, the collaboration says.

Halzen first presented the idea in 1988, Forbes reported. A smaller predecessor experiment at the South Pole, known as AMANDA, tested the approach in the 1990s before IceCube was funded and built.

From a Long Shot to a New Kind of Astronomy

Halzen has been candid that success was far from certain. "When we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself," he said after the announcement, according to Morocco World News.

IceCube delivered. In 2013, the collaboration reported the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos coming from outside the solar system. In 2018, it traced a neutrino to a distant blazar, a galaxy with a feeding supermassive black hole. In 2022, it identified neutrinos streaming from the active galaxy NGC 1068, and in 2023, it produced the first image of the Milky Way made with neutrinos rather than light.

Those results opened the field now called neutrino astronomy. Combined with traditional telescopes and gravitational-wave detectors, it lets scientists study the same cosmic event through several kinds of signals at once, a practice known as multimessenger astronomy.

Eva Olsson of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences described neutrinos as messengers that can carry information about distant galaxies and violent astrophysical processes, Morocco World News reported.

Halzen said the most important findings may still lie ahead. "This is just an introduction to the science; the astronomy is still to come," he said.

Antarctic Science and the People Behind It

IceCube is operated at the National Science Foundation's Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station with an international collaboration of universities and laboratories. The prize recognizes Halzen as its leader, but the observatory depends on drillers, engineers, technicians and researchers who winter over at one of the coldest, most isolated places on Earth.

The Nobel also highlights the scientific return from Antarctica itself. The continent's ice is valuable not only as a record of past climate but as a natural laboratory, and IceCube shows how its physical properties, clarity, depth and stability can be put to work for astronomy.

What the detector cannot yet do is pin down where most cosmic neutrinos come from. Only a handful of individual sources have been identified so far, and researchers say many more years of data, along with planned upgrades, will be needed to map the rest.

Halzen, born in Tienen, Belgium, has been on the Wisconsin faculty since 1972 and earned his doctorate at the University of Louvain, Forbes reported.

The remaining Nobel announcements continue through the week. The bottom line: a detector frozen deep in the South Pole has turned the most elusive particle in physics into a new way to see the universe, and the scientist who imagined it in 1988 has now received science's highest honor.

What Readers Want to Know

Who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics?

Francis Halzen, a physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, won the full prize for his work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space.

What is a neutrino?

A neutrino is a nearly massless particle with no electric charge. Trillions pass through each person every second without interacting, which makes them very hard to detect.

Why was IceCube built in Antarctic ice?

Catching neutrinos requires a huge, clear and dark volume of material. The deep ice at the South Pole provides all three, letting sensors spot the faint blue light made when a neutrino hits an atom.

How big is IceCube?

It spans one cubic kilometer of ice, with 5,160 sensors placed between 1,450 and 2,450 meters below the surface.

What has IceCube discovered?

It found the first evidence of high-energy cosmic neutrinos in 2013, linked neutrinos to a distant blazar in 2018 and to the galaxy NGC 1068 in 2022, and mapped the Milky Way in neutrinos in 2023.

How much is the prize worth?

The prize is 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million. Halzen will receive it in Stockholm on Dec. 10.
